findings.failure_scenario: An in-use schema S has a parent DictionarySchema/ArraySchema whose element type E extends an otherwise-unreferenced ObjectSchema B, and B's children relation is absent (the same children-relation condition this fix relies on for the direct-parent Dog/Golden case). The stream at line 139 only scans parents of the pre-existing schemasInUse members; E enters schemasInUse only at line 156, after the scan, and no later pass ever iterates E (it is not a property/request/response/exception schema). B therefore stays in schemasNotInUse, gets removed by the removeIf at line 173, and the generated code 'class E extends B' no longer compiles — the exact class of breakage this PR fixes for direct ObjectSchema parents, left open one level of indirection deeper.
findings.summary: The new parent-preservation logic is not transitive for collection parents: an ObjectSchema element reached only via a Dictionary/Array parent is added to schemasInUse after the parent-scan stream is already consumed, and every tryCleanup pass recomputes the identical sets, so that element's own ObjectSchema ancestors are never protected from removal.

findings.failure_scenario: Maintainability cost: the statement has no observable effect in any pass, yet it implies discriminator schemas are retained as in-use for subsequent processing. If the author's intent was to keep discriminator schemas in the in-use set across passes (e.g., so their own parents or discriminators would be protected later), that protection silently does not happen because schemasInUse is a method-local set discarded when tryCleanup returns; the line should be removed or the intended transitive use implemented.
findings.summary: schemasInUse.addAll(discriminators) is a no-op: the local schemasInUse set is never read after this statement (tryCleanup only uses schemasNotInUse/choicesSchemasNotInUse from line 171 on) and is rebuilt from scratch on every one of the up-to-5 process() passes, so the discriminator schemas are protected solely by the two removeAll calls above it.
